supplement

/SUP-luh-ment/ — starts like 'supper' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To supplement is to build something up by adding an extra amount or piece to it.

Farmers supplement the poor soil with compost to help the crops thrive.

Example

Marcus loved his history textbook, but it barely covered ancient trade routes. So he supplemented it with documentaries, museum visits, and a podcast, layering extra sources on top of the book.

To 'replace' the book would mean discarding it; to supplement it means keeping it and adding extra elements on top.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

augment: Augment means to make something greater by adding to it — you augment a budget or a staff, and the result is more of the same thing. To supplement is to answer a lack: you add an extra, often different, element because what exists cannot do the job alone.

bolster: Bolster means to strengthen or support something with additions, the way fresh evidence bolsters an argument — the aim is firmness. To supplement aims at completeness: you add an extra amount or piece because the original, however sturdy, still falls short of what is needed.

enrich: Enrich means to improve something's quality by adding to it — a soil, a story, a life made better. To supplement targets amount and coverage instead: the original is not bad, just insufficient, so you build it up with an extra piece to fill the gap.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reduce: to make smaller or less

deplete: to use up or drain away

Where it sits · how big the alteration is

tweak → supplement → transform

tweak vs. supplement: Tweak is weaker than supplement — a tweak changes only a tiny detail, while supplementing adds a whole extra element.

transform vs. supplement: Transform is stronger than supplement — supplementing adds to what's already there, but transforming changes the thing completely.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — sup- (sub-): up from below (Latin)

root — ple-: to fill (Latin)

suffix — -ment: result or means of (Latin)

Put it together: Latin supplere meant 'to fill up from below.' To supplement is to pour more in — filling up what is lacking until something is fuller and better.

Use the root in a new word: replenish: The manager reminded the night crew to replenish the shelves before closing.
